description: A small, soft, creeping herb that spreads by slender runners rooting at the nodes. It has long-stalked, round to kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges, usually rising from the nodes in tufts, and tiny reddish-purple flowers clustered close to the ground.
cultural_significance: The Sanskrit name means 'frog-leaf', after the shape of its leaves. It is regarded in Ayurveda as a Medhya Rasayana (intellect-promoting tonic), and in many regions it is confused or interchanged with Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri). It is not a Vedic-era plant by name; it is prominent in later texts and folk traditions, including Sri Lankan cooking where it is eaten as a leaf salad (gotu kola sambol).
habitat: Moist, shady ground, stream banks, paddy-field bunds, damp lawns and forest floors in tropical and subtropical regions, from sea level to mid hills.

uses.title: Memory and nervine tonic
uses.detail: Described in Ayurveda as a Medhya herb traditionally given to support memory, mental clarity and calmness, particularly in older people and students.

uses.title: Skin disorders and wound healing
uses.detail: Crushed fresh leaf or leaf paste is traditionally applied to minor wounds, burns and skin eruptions, and taken internally as a skin tonic.

uses.title: Fever and urinary complaints
uses.detail: Leaf juice or decoction is traditionally used in fevers and in burning urination, in keeping with its cooling character.

uses.title: Leaf salad and household tonic
uses.detail: Eaten fresh in salads and chutneys in South and South-East Asia as a cooling green with a mildly bitter taste.

uses.title: Wound and vein research
uses.detail: Triterpenoid-rich Centella extracts such as TECA have been studied for wound and scar healing and for chronic venous insufficiency; evidence is mixed and preliminary.

preparations.name: Swarasa (fresh leaf juice)
preparations.method: Wash fresh leaves, crush and press out the juice; traditionally taken with honey or buttermilk.
preparations.note: Small quantities only; practitioner guidance advised.

preparations.name: Kwatha (decoction)
preparations.method: Boil the whole plant in water until reduced, strain and sip warm.
preparations.note: Traditionally used in fever and skin complaints.

preparations.name: Churna (dried leaf powder)
preparations.method: Shade-dry the herb and grind to a fine powder; taken with warm water, milk or honey.
preparations.note: Commonly sold as a nervine tonic powder.

preparations.name: Leaf paste for external use
preparations.method: Grind fresh leaves with a little water into a paste and apply to minor wounds or skin patches.
preparations.note: Patch-test first; avoid on deep or infected wounds.

preparations.name: Mandukaparni ghrita or tea
preparations.method: Ghee medicated with the herb by the classical ghrita method, or a mild infusion of a few leaves in hot water.
preparations.note: Ghrita is made by trained manufacturers; the infusion is a mild daily drink.

precautions: May cause drowsiness, so use caution with sedatives or sleep medicines. Topical use can cause contact dermatitis or skin irritation in sensitive people. Reports link prolonged high-dose use with liver problems, so people with liver disease or those taking liver-affecting medicines should consult a doctor. May affect blood sugar and cholesterol, so people on diabetes medicines should be careful. Avoid medicinal use in pregnancy and breastfeeding unless advised by a practitioner. Do not confuse with Bacopa monnieri, which is also sold as Brahmi.

cultivation.climate: Warm, humid tropical to subtropical; tolerates mild cool spells but not hard frost
cultivation.sunlight: Partial shade; leaves scorch in harsh midday sun
cultivation.water: Keep constantly moist; tolerates shallow wet ground
cultivation.propagation: Runners or stem cuttings with a node, which root readily; also seeds
cultivation.harvest: Cut leafy runners every 2-3 months; regrows quickly

conservation_status: Not threatened; widespread and weedy, though wild collection for the herbal trade is heavy in some regions.
fun_fact: Its Sanskrit name Mandukaparni means 'frog leaf', and a stretch of damp ground can be covered by a single plant sending out runners that root wherever they touch.
